title: AI is difficult to use for auto-trading
author: Ok-Variation3247
selftext: It's easy to find a strategy that when backtested comes back with a high win rate in your favor. However...when you forward test those strategies with real or paper money, you find out quickly that most auto strategies fail. I think a.i can be used to make helpful alerts for conditions but actually waiting for entry and exit conditions and executing the entire roundtrip on auto-pilot is not something a.i. is good at, at this point. I think it comes down to not being able to know when to exit a trade that's not a mathematical equation which is hard for it to understand and execute. It's missing that human feel of sensing when to exit a trade.

comments.author: evilistics
comments.body: Are you focusing on one ticker on one timeframe? If you are looking for a strategy that works across multiple tickers then that is a dead end. Quants would test thousands to millions of settings per Strat per ticker and time frame to find an edge. AI is not going to just magically find the specific settings for that ticker and time frame when you feed it a paper or Strat from youtube. Get it to create a system to test every variable and find the one that works in a walk forward setting. You'll find AI can easily find something that looks good on a backtest but when it's run live it falls apart. If your Strat can't be backtested and walk forwarded in a Sim then you'll have to run thousands of realtime, live trading Sims and sort them by success rate. Trading is a numbers game, winners are rare and hard to find. You'll need to sort through the 99% losers and even if you find winners, they will often plateau and fall off eventually which is why the hunt for winners has to be a constant effort. It's also why strata that walk forwarded fine in a backtest 2 years ago will fail now. Markets change and so do the settings needed to exploit them.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: The gap between backtest and forward results is mostly about overfitting and costs, not a missing human feel: a high win rate in a backtest usually comes from many variants tried on the same data, optimistic fills and no fees, so it shrinks when the rule meets live prices. Exits can be written as rules too (a stop, a target, a time limit or a trailing rule), and a deterministic script that executes them is usually more reliable than asking a model to decide each exit. A useful split is to let AI handle alerts, research and code, and keep entries, exits and size in plain rules with hard limits, then forward test a frozen version and compare it with a simple baseline and with random entries using the same exits. Backtest Labs at Cymetica is one place to see how strategy results are compared before anyone runs them live.

replies.author: Ok-Variation3247
replies.body: Yes as I've stated previously, it all sounds good in practice until you forward test then it all falls apart. Ai is best used for strategy discovery, entry opportunities but its not good at the entire round trip. Even exits can be tricky, while programmable - it doesn't mean P+L consistency.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: That's fair, and a programmable exit doesn't guarantee consistent P&L, because the exit rule still has to be tested like any other part of the strategy. The useful check is to run the same entries with several exit rules on data the rules weren't built on, and see how much of the result comes from the entries and how much from the exits. If the result changes sign with small exit changes, there's no edge in the exit, and the forward test is the right place to find that out.
